intro: About 900 years ago, a few knights in Jerusalem made a promise. They would guard travelers on dangerous roads. They would also live like monks. People called them the Knights Templar. In time, they grew rich and famous across Europe.

Then, one Friday morning in 1307, the king of France had them arrested. Their story ended in trials, a lost parchment and many legends. Some legends are still told today, about treasure, curses and secret survival.

In this unit, you will learn how the Templars lived and why they fell. You will read real records from the time. You will practice a skill historians use every day: sorting what the evidence shows from what a story only claims.
bigQuestion: How can we tell what really happened to the Knights Templar from the legends people tell about them?

timeline.t: Christian armies from Europe take Jerusalem in the First Crusade.
Hugh of Payns and a few knights begin guarding pilgrims in Jerusalem.
The Council of Troyes gives the Templars their written Rule.
The Temple Church in London is blessed.
Acre falls, and the Templars lose their main home in the Holy Land.
On Friday, 13 October, King Philip IV has the Templars in France arrested.
Three cardinals forgive Templar leaders at Chinon Castle.
Pope Clement V ends the Templar order without a guilty verdict.
Jacques de Molay, the last Grand Master, is put to death in Paris.
American Masonic Knights Templar, inspired by the old order, meet in Chicago.
Barbara Frale finds the misfiled Chinon Parchment in the Vatican's archive.

words.d: a person who travels to a holy place to pray
a group of people who live by the same religious rules and promises
a written set of rules for how members of a religious order live
a serious promise, often made to God
a long, loose cloak worn over other clothes
money or treasure left with someone to keep safe
a claim that someone did something wrong
to say that you did something wrong
forgiveness of sins given by a church leader
a place that keeps old papers and records safe
something made at the time by people who were there
a story told often that may or may not be true

test.q: Why did the first Templars come together?
choices: To build ships for the king
To guard pilgrims on the roads to Jerusalem
test.why: Hugh of Payns and his friends promised to guard pilgrims on dangerous roads.

test.q: Where did the name Templar come from?
choices: Their rooms on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem
The name of their first leader
test.why: The king gave them rooms on the Temple Mount, where people thought Solomon's Temple had stood.

test.q: What was the Rule of the Templars?
choices: A written set of rules for how the brothers lived
A law made by the king of France
test.why: The Rule, given at Troyes about 1129, told the brothers how to live.

test.q: Which three promises did Templars make?
choices: To fight, to farm and to sail
To travel, to trade and to build
To read, to write and to teach
To own nothing, not to marry, and to obey
test.why: Templars vowed to own nothing of their own, not to marry, and to obey their leaders.

choices: A white mantle with a red cross
A black robe with a crown
test.why: Knights wore white mantles, and in the 1140s a red cross was added.

test.q: How did the Templars do an early kind of banking?
choices: They kept deposits safe and moved money between their houses
They made gold coins for Rome
test.why: The Templars kept money safe for people and helped move it over long distances.

test.q: Most Templar brothers in Europe were ...
choices: people who ran farms and sent help east
test.why: Most brothers in Europe ran farms and sent money and horses to the Holy Land.

choices: The Templars in France were arrested
test.why: At dawn that day, King Philip IV's officers arrested the Templars across France.

test.q: Why did Philip IV's order use words like horrible and bitter?
choices: To make readers angry and afraid before seeing proof
test.why: These are loaded words, chosen to stir up feelings before any proof is shown.

test.q: Which is a primary source about the Templar trials?
choices: The records of the papal commission, 1309-1311
test.why: The commission's records were written at the time by people who were there.

test.q: What did Barbara Frale find in 2001?
test.why: Frale found the misfiled Chinon Parchment in the Vatican's archive.

test.q: How did the pope end the order in 1312?
choices: By a court that found it guilty
By his own power, without a guilty verdict
By a vote of the knights
By selling it to the king
test.why: Vox in excelso ended the order by the pope's power, not by a court's judgment.

test.q: Who received most Templar lands after 1312?
test.why: The pope gave most Templar lands to the Hospitallers.

test.q: Which is a legend with no proof from the time?
choices: Hidden Templar treasure that is still waiting to be found
test.why: No Templar treasure has ever been found, and no record backs the story.

test.q: How are the 1880 Chicago Knights Templar different from the medieval Templars?
choices: They were older than the medieval Templars
They were inspired by the old order but not descended from it
test.why: The Chicago group admired the old Templars, but no line of members links them.

write.prompt: Were the Templars guilty of the charges against them? Write a paragraph that answers the question. Use two or three facts or sources from this unit, such as the confessions, the Chinon Parchment or the pope's 1312 decision. Explain how each one supports your answer.
tips: Start with one clear sentence that gives your answer.
Name each source you use, like the Chinon Parchment.
Tell how the confessions were given before you trust them.
Say what someone who disagrees might point to.
Use unit words like charge, confess and evidence.
